findings.explanation:
Big objects are Salesforce's platform-native store for a long-lived historical archive: they give "consistent performance, whether you have 1 million records, 100 million, or even 1 billion", and "Historical archive" is one of the three use cases the Big Objects guide names. A 10-year compliance retention of case history is exactly that shape, and it stays inside the org.
A plain custom object (C) keeps the rows in the transactional store, which is the load the LDV guide's whole remedy is meant to reduce; buying storage (B) does the same thing more expensively.
Option A is not as empty as it looks — Salesforce Archive is a real, separately purchased product that runs archiving policies to "regularly offload inactive records, files, and attachments from production". It is rejected here because it is a licensed add-on rather than something you configure in the org, and because big objects keep the data queryable on-platform for the full retention window.
Worth knowing before you build it: Salesforce does not recommend reporting straight off a big object. View Big Object Data in Reports and Dashboards says that at that scale "it's not practical to build reports or dashboards directly from that data", and has you extract a representative subset with Bulk API into a custom object first.

Contacts to Multiple Accounts, backed by the AccountContactRelation object, lets one Contact be associated with many Accounts. The relation carries an IsDirect flag that distinguishes the contact's own primary account from the additional, indirect ones, so a single customer record can sit against both the Residential and the Business Account without being duplicated.
Person Accounts (B) would create a second, separate consumer record for someone already modelled as a Contact. Parent Account (D) models one organisation under another, not one person spanning two accounts. "Individual objects" (C) is not the mechanism for this — Individual is the privacy/consent record, not a customer-identity join.

Heroku Connect with Heroku Postgres (A) and a middleware/ESB integration (D) both do genuine bidirectional, near-real-time sync between two orgs. The cross-org adapter for Salesforce Connect (E) is the third: it "uses Lightning Platform REST API calls to access records in other Salesforce orgs", surfacing them as external objects that are read on demand rather than copied, so each org sees the other's current Opportunities.
A scheduled daily Apex push (C) fails the near-real-time requirement outright. A third-party AppExchange tool (B) might work but names no mechanism, so it is the weakest of the four plausible options.
findings.note: Answer stands. The old explanation ended by asserting that the cross-org adapter is read-only, so 'bidirectional' could only mean mutual viewing. Salesforce documents writable external objects for Salesforce Connect — the Apex Developer Guide's Writable External Objects page points at 'Writable External Objects Considerations for Salesforce Connect—All Adapters' — so that blanket denial is not supported.

findings.explanation:
Person Accounts model an individual who is not an employee of some parent organisation, which is what both the patients and the doctors are here; payment providers are organisations, so they are business Accounts. That gives every actor a top-level record that can be related to the others through junction objects, and lets each carry its own sharing.
Modelling doctors as Contacts (B) hangs each doctor under one parent Account, which fits a practice roster but not a doctor who must relate to many independent patients. A and D mix the two in ways that leave one actor type without a workable relationship path.
This one is a design-judgment item rather than a documented rule: Salesforce publishes no page that assigns these three actors to these three object types, and Contacts to Multiple Accounts would let a Contact-based doctor relate to many accounts too. Treat it as the best of the offered models, not as a settled fact.

Routing both CRMs through SAP (C) keeps one hub as the system of record and avoids a direct legacy-CRM-to-Salesforce link, which during a phased cutover is where circular updates and duplicates come from. An MDM solution (D) adds the governed golden record and survivorship rules across all three systems, which is what actually keeps them agreeing rather than merely connected.
A is the anti-pattern the other two avoid; B drops the legacy CRM out of the picture entirely while it is still in use.
This is an architecture-judgment item. Salesforce documents the integration mechanisms but publishes no page that picks hub-and-spoke over point-to-point for this scenario, so treat the pair as the best-reasoned answer rather than a cited rule.

Outbound Messaging is the declarative real-time push: it "allows you to specify that changes to fields within Salesforce can cause messages with field values to be sent to designated external servers", so a Closed/Won stage change fires a SOAP message to the ERP with no code.
Nightly polling (C) and an hourly batch (D) both fail the real-time requirement. MDM (A) decides which system owns a value; it is not an event-driven push.
One currency note: Salesforce ended support for Workflow Rules on 31 December 2025, so a new build would fire the same Outbound Message action from a record-triggered flow. Existing rules keep running, and the mechanism named in the answer is unchanged.

The LDV guide's Searching best practices state both answers almost word for word: "Use single-object searches for greater speed and accuracy" (A) and "Keep searches specific and avoid using wildcards, if possible. For example, search with Michael instead of Mi*" (B).
Searching IN ALL FIELDS (D) does the opposite — it widens the search surface. There is no SOSL option to ignore custom indexes (C); the search index is not something a query opts out of.

Serial mode exists for exactly one reason, and the Bulk API guidelines name it: use it when parallel mode produces lock timeouts you cannot fix by reorganising batches. Loading a million Orders spread across shared Accounts is the classic case, because every child write locks its parent (B).
Option D describes locks already eliminated and managed — which removes the only reason to accept serial mode's lower throughput. Batch counts (A, C) are throughput knobs, not the reason to switch modes.
Before reaching for serial mode, the guide's cheaper fix is to group the batch by parent: "If you organize AccountTeamMember records by AccountId so that all records referencing the same account are in a single batch, you minimize the risk of lock contention by multiple batches."

At 100 million rows a month, a custom big object is the only on-platform store that holds the data: big objects give "consistent performance, whether you have 1 million records, 100 million, or even 1 billion", and the guide names both "360° view of the customer" and "Historical archive" as their purpose. A plain custom object (D) is a transactional-store object and does not survive that growth rate.
Big objects are a Lightning Platform construct defined through Metadata API or Setup — there is no such thing as creating one "in Einstein Analytics" (C). Pointing the analytics tool straight at the point-of-sale system (B) leaves the data outside Salesforce entirely, which the requirement rules out.
One caveat worth carrying into the design: Salesforce does not have you report directly off a big object at this scale. View Big Object Data in Reports and Dashboards has you extract a representative subset with Bulk API into a custom object and report on that.

Standard custom objects in a header/detail shape (C) model a request with up to five line items cleanly, and an archiving process that moves data off-platform past the three-year window is the LDV guide's own advice: "Use a data-tiering strategy that spreads data across multiple objects, and brings in data on demand from another object or external store", plus "Reduce the amount of data by archiving unused records."
Flattening five items into five lookup fields (B, D) hard-codes a limit into the schema and breaks as soon as a sixth item appears.
The reason to reject the external-object designs (A, B) is not that reports are impossible — Salesforce Connect does support reports on external objects. It is that every read is a live callout to Heroku, so three years of report history depends on that system's latency and availability, and reports that include an external object fetch a bounded number of rows for the primary object. For a reporting requirement over the org's own transactional data, keeping it on-platform and tiering the old rows out is the simpler design.
findings.note: Answer stands. The old explanation rejected the external-object options on the ground that "external objects cannot be reported on natively" — an invented absence. Salesforce publishes an article titled "Salesforce Connect Support for Reports"; external objects can be used in custom report types, with limitations.

findings.explanation:
A Lookup relationship marked required, with its delete behaviour set to Restrict, satisfies all three requirements at once. Metadata API documents that setting on the field: "Restrict—Prevents the record from being deleted if it's in a lookup relationship." Making the lookup required forces the association; Restrict blocks deletion of a Product, Sender, or Receiver that a Shipment still points at.
Master-detail (C, D) fails the third requirement by construction: detail records "inherit the master's sharing and security settings", so Shipment could not keep a sharing model separate from its parents.
A VLOOKUP formula (A) is a validation-rule function, not a relationship, and creates no link at all.

Delete is an all-or-nothing profile permission plus OWD; neither can express "everyone may edit, only the owner may delete". A trigger can: Apex triggers fire "Before or after a delete operation", so a before delete trigger comparing UserInfo.getUserId() to OwnerId and calling addError() is the enforcement point.
Removing Delete from the profile (C) blocks the owner as well. Public Read Only (B) would take away the org-wide edit access the stem requires. Validation rules (D) are part of the save order for insert, update, and upsert — the order of execution documents no delete path for them, so nothing fires when a record is deleted.

A first governance assessment establishes authority and then maps the current state: executive sponsorship sets enterprise data strategy, scope, and the mandate to enforce it (C), and business units together with IT are who can describe the operational systems and data models actually in use (D).
Project velocity (A) and database performance metrics (B) are delivery and operations concerns; neither tells you what data exists, who owns it, or what the enterprise wants from it.
Salesforce publishes governance guidance rather than a prescribed sequence of first steps, so this item rests on general data-governance practice rather than on a rule that a specific page states.

The LDV guide ranks the operations directly: "Use the fastest operation possible—insert() is fastest, update() is next, and upsert() is next after that." Because UC already knows which 200,000 rows are new and which 100,000 exist, splitting the work into a pure insert and a pure update (D) uses the two fastest operations and skips upsert's per-row external-ID match entirely.
Upsert (C) is the convenient answer and the slower one. Deleting and reloading everything (B) throws away record ids, history, and anything related to them. The Streaming API (A) delivers event messages; it is not a load mechanism.

A staging database is where two legacy sources can be reconciled against each other before either one reaches Salesforce: key both on External IDs, merge and cleanse there, then load once. External ID fields carry the cross-system key and are indexed, which is what makes the merge and the later upsert possible.
Duplicate rules (B) and upsert (D) both do their work inside the target org, so the first load still puts unresolved duplicates and unvalidated values into Salesforce. Migrating one database into the other (A) cleans nothing; it just moves the problem.
Salesforce documents the mechanisms rather than prescribing this sequence, so treat the staging-first pattern as the best-reasoned option here rather than a rule a specific page states.

System of record is a governance decision, not something the integration topology reveals. Three systems all write Account and Opportunity here, so no mechanical rule picks a winner: reviewing each data flow with the business users who understand which system is authoritative for which attribute (D) is the only approach that produces a defensible answer per object or field.
Origination (A) ignores that a downstream system may be authoritative for values it owns. Last-writer-wins (C) is an accident of scheduling. "Whoever updates it" (B) collapses the moment two systems update the same field — which is the situation described.
Salesforce publishes governance guidance rather than a rule that decides this, so this rests on general data-governance practice.

Integrating a third-party address validation and enrichment service (C) is the strategy that scales: it verifies and standardises millions of addresses against authoritative reference data automatically. Phoning each business (A) or staffing a manual validation team (B) does not scale to several million records by any reading.
Option D is the exam's second answer, and it names a product Salesforce has retired. Data.com appears in Salesforce's Past Product & Feature Retirements list, and the Data.com Clean setup article no longer exists. Keep D as the keyed answer because that is what the item tests, but a current implementation would use a third-party enrichment service or Data Cloud rather than Data.com Clean.
findings.note: Answer stands as the exam keys it, but the item is stale: keyed option D names Data.com Clean, which Salesforce has retired and which appears in its Past Product & Feature Retirements list.

findings.explanation:
An enterprise governance body needs members with definitional authority over data. Data Domain Stewards (B) own the quality rules and definitions for their domain, and Analytics/BI Owners (A) own the enterprise metrics those definitions have to serve — between them they can decide what a field means and what "good" looks like across business units.
Salesforce Administrators (C) implement decisions inside one org, and Operational Data Users (D) consume the data; both are essential stakeholders and neither sets cross-business-unit policy.
Salesforce publishes governance guidance rather than a prescribed committee roster, so this item rests on general data-governance practice rather than a documented rule.

Filtering on indexed fields (A) is the LDV guide's own reporting advice — "Use report filters that emphasize the use of standard or custom indexed fields" — because a selective, indexed filter is what keeps the optimizer off a full scan. Skinny tables (C) are the other documented remedy: Salesforce builds them "to contain frequently used fields and to avoid joins", and they omit soft-deleted records, so a wide, high-volume object reports much faster.
Sharing a report with fewer people (D) changes nothing about how long the query runs.
Two things to hold on to about this item. Option C misstates how skinny tables work: they are per object, not per report, and "You can't create, access, or modify skinny tables yourself" — you request them from Salesforce Customer Support. And option B is not really wrong: the LDV guide documents Divisions as "a means of partitioning the data of large deployments to reduce the number of records returned by queries and reports", for orgs over a million records in a single object with more than 35 licences. Divisions are a heavier, org-wide commitment than the keyed pair, which is why they are not the answer here, but the option set treats a documented remedy as a distractor.
findings.note: Answer stands, but the item is defective in two ways: keyed option C describes creating a skinny table per report, which nobody can do (skinny tables are per object and are created by Salesforce Customer Support), and distractor B names Divisions, which the LDV guide documents as a real remedy for exactly this problem.

findings.explanation:
Keeping disparate systems in agreement takes two things: a mechanism that moves the data, and a rule that decides which value wins. Integrating Salesforce with the ERP environment (A) is the mechanism; an MDM strategy (C) supplies the single source of truth and the survivorship rules, without which two-way sync just propagates conflicts.
Workbench (B) is an ad-hoc tool for one-off admin work, not a synchronisation mechanism. Reports and dashboards (D) observe divergence after the fact; they never resolve it.
This is an architecture-judgment item — Salesforce documents the integration options but publishes no page that names this pair.

Salesforce Shield bundles Event Monitoring, Platform Encryption, Field Audit Trail, and Data Detect. Three of the customer's mandates land inside that bundle: detailed monitoring of user activity is Event Monitoring (A); blocking exports is a Transaction Security Policy, which Salesforce describes as automatically blocking risky user actions to prevent data loss (D); and protecting PII and financial records at rest is Platform Encryption (E).
The other two requirements are real but are met elsewhere. Restricting access by geography (B) is done with profile Login IP Ranges and org trusted IP ranges, not with Shield. Withholding PII from sales users (C) is field-level security and sharing.

The Skinny Tables page states all three keyed properties. They "omit soft-deleted records" (A). Salesforce "can create skinny tables to contain frequently used fields and to avoid joins" (B) — the join it avoids is between the base table and the custom-field table. And "Skinny tables are kept in sync with their source tables when the source tables are modified" (C), which is what makes them usable without a refresh step.
Option D is the inverse of the documented rule: "Skinny tables can't contain fields from other objects."
Option E is simply wrong on its number. The documented cap is "Skinny tables can contain a maximum of 200 columns", not 100.
findings.note: Answer stands. The old explanation accepted option E's "100-column cap" as a real limit that merely wasn't a performance driver. The documented maximum is 200 columns, so E is false on its face, not just irrelevant.

findings.explanation:
Loading a large, regular feed of child time-entry records into a privately-shared parent makes Salesforce recalculate sharing as each batch lands, on top of recomputing the parent's roll-up summaries. The LDV guide's remedy for the sharing half is explicit: "Use the defer sharing calculation permission to defer sharing calculations until after all data has been loaded", then run one recalculation.
Replacing roll-up summary fields with workflow (B) or triggers (C) swaps a platform-maintained aggregate for custom automation that fires on every one of those inserts — more work per record, not less. External IDs (D) are how you resolve the parent reference during the load; they do nothing about the recalculation cost that is the problem here.
findings.note: Item defect: the stem says "as shown in the image" but the data-model exhibit did not survive scraping. The stem's prose describes the model well enough to answer, so the question is still answerable — but the image is not coming back.

findings.explanation:
An ETL tool transforms mismatched data types in flight — that is the T in ETL — so it maps legacy types to Salesforce types, cleanses, and loads in one pipeline (C). Standing up a staging database first (A) or writing stored procedures against one (B) adds infrastructure to do work the ETL layer already does. Data Loader (D) reads a CSV and writes it; it performs no type transformation, so a mismatched source would simply fail on load.
This is a tooling-judgment item: Salesforce documents the load mechanisms rather than ranking ETL against a staging database for this scenario.

Migrating a relational schema starts by deciding what actually needs to live in Salesforce rather than porting the whole database (A), mapping the elements that survive onto Salesforce objects (B), and then realising that model with custom objects and fields (E).
Option C is a strict subset of B — mapping to custom objects is one outcome of mapping to objects, since much of a legacy model lands on standard objects such as Account, Contact, and Opportunity. That is why B is keyed over C.
Be aware this item is loose: option D, analysing the legacy model with its application owner, is at least as defensible a third choice as E, and the two are not mutually exclusive. Treat A and B as the solid pair and the third slot as the item's weak point.
findings.note: Item defect: option C is a strict subset of keyed option B, and distractor D (analyse the legacy data model with its owner) is at least as defensible as keyed option E. The key is the exam's, but the third choice is not decidable from the stem.

findings.explanation:
Three things in this stem only MDM delivers together: a different system of record per entity (Salesforce for Leads, the OMS for Accounts and Contacts), deliberate attribute divergence ("John Doe" in one system and "Johnny Doe" in the other), and a consolidated store that cross-references the same real customer across systems.
Point-to-point synchronisation (A, B) fails the second requirement outright — whichever side writes last flattens the other's name — and produces no cross-reference store. The Streaming API (D) delivers event messages one way; it reconciles nothing.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents the integration mechanisms rather than naming MDM as the answer to this scenario.

Reporting Snapshots are the native mechanism for exactly this problem: they "let you report on historical data" by saving "tabular or summary report results to fields on a custom object" on a schedule. Snapshot the trend data, then purge the detail rows behind it (B). Scheduled batch Apex that rolls detail into a summary object and deletes the originals (A) reaches the same place under your own control.
Data Loader (C) extracts and loads; it does not aggregate, so that round trip cannot produce the summary the stem needs.
Option D is not the empty distractor it once was. Salesforce Archive is a real, separately purchased product whose policies "regularly offload inactive records, files, and attachments from production" and shrink the storage footprint. It is not keyed here because it addresses only half the requirement — storage — and does nothing for the historical trend reporting that is the other half.
findings.note: Answer stands. The old explanation rejected option D on the ground that "there is no general native 'Salesforce Archiving feature'" — an invented absence. Salesforce Archive exists as a purchasable product with automated archiving policies that remove records from production.

findings.explanation:
Salesforce names option D's design as an anti-pattern by its own worked example. Parent-Child Data Skew describes skew as "a large number of child records (10,000 or more)" on one parent, and illustrates it with "a customer with hundreds of thousands of contacts all assigned to one dummy account" — which is precisely what loading a million consumers as Contacts under a single Account produces. Every insert in the load contends for the same parent row, and every later visibility change forces Salesforce to scan the whole child set, so the design fails the stem's own "avoid data loading issues" test. Even the LDV guide's bucket-account workaround says to "set up several dummy accounts and distribute the contacts among them", never one.
One Account and one Contact per consumer (C) is the standard business-account B2C model when Person Accounts are not on the table — it is the same shape Person Accounts create internally. No parent carries more than one child, so there is no skew and no load contention, and both standard objects keep their full functionality.
A custom Individual_Consumer__c object (A) throws away everything that works on Contact. Loading consumers as Accounts with no Contacts (B) leaves nothing to attach activities, campaign members, or cases to.
findings.note: Key moved D to C. The deck keyed the single-bucket-account pattern, which is the exact configuration Salesforce's Parent-Child Data Skew page uses as its example of what not to do ("hundreds of thousands of contacts all assigned to one dummy account"), and which causes the load contention the stem asks to avoid. The LDV guide's own bucket workaround specifies several dummy accounts, not one.

findings.explanation:
The distinguishing requirement is transformation, not volume: Org B has different objects, fields, and picklist values, so every record has to be remapped in flight. An ETL tool is built for that — extract, transform against the new model, load — and can be re-run repeatedly as the mapping is refined across a two-month window.
Data Import Wizard (B) is limited to a small subset of objects and record counts and performs no transformation. A hand-written Bulk API script (C) and the Salesforce CLI (D) can both move three million records, but you would be building the mapping, value translation, and error handling that the ETL layer already provides.
This is a tooling-judgment item — Salesforce documents the mechanisms rather than ranking them for an org split.

Leads arriving from many sources will be uneven no matter how carefully the forms are built, so completeness has to come from somewhere other than the source. An external data provider appends authoritative company profile and location attributes automatically as records land (C), which is the only option that scales with lead volume.
Asking reps to look the data up (A) and shipping exports to another team (D) both put a human in the path of every record. Reporting on blanks (B) measures the gap accurately and closes none of it.
This is a data-quality judgment item; Salesforce documents enrichment products rather than naming this as the answer.

Collapsing Venue from a related object into a picklist on Conference trades relational integrity for a value list, and the consequences are all about how that value list behaves under volume. Loading hundreds of thousands of Conferences a year through the Bulk API puts every Venue value through picklist handling on insert (C), and a picklist is inline-editable from a standard list view (D), so a value can be changed in bulk by anyone with edit access and no relationship to protect it.
Master-detail limits (A) stop applying the moment the relationship is removed, and org storage (B) goes down, not up, when two objects become one.
Be aware this is a weakly constructed item. Neither keyed consideration is stated as a documented rule anywhere in Salesforce's picklist or Bulk API guidance, and the two remaining options are rejected on relevance rather than on any documented fact. The underlying design point — that twenty stable Venues are better modelled as a picklist than as a lookup that 20,000 records each point at — is sound and is documented, as concentrating that many children on one lookup target is textbook lookup skew.
findings.note: Item defect: neither keyed consideration (Bulk API picklist limitations, list-view inline editing) corresponds to a documented Salesforce rule, and the distractors are rejected on relevance rather than fact. The key is the exam's; the item is not decidable from documentation.

findings.explanation:
PK Chunking is built for this exact volume. The Bulk API guide says it "splits bulk queries on large tables into chunks based on the record IDs, or primary keys, of the queried records", and recommends enabling it "when querying tables with more than 10 million records or when a bulk query consistently times out". At 100 million records both conditions apply.
Bulk API in parallel mode without chunking (D) still issues one query across the whole table, which is what times out. Successive REST queries (B) page through the same full scan more slowly. A third-party tool (A) runs on the same API and inherits the same limits.

Moving users between territories rewrites group membership, and Salesforce "locks the tables holding group membership information during updates to prevent incompatible simultaneous updates" — which is where the lock errors come from. Granular locking is the mechanism that narrows those locks: it allows "some group maintenance operations to proceed simultaneously if there's no hierarchical or other relationship between the roles or groups involved", so separate role hierarchies and territory-free groups stop blocking each other.
Reducing concurrency (A) trades the error for a slower process. Splunk (C) and more CPU (D) address neither the lock semantics nor the tables involved.
One currency note: Salesforce now documents granular locking as the default behaviour rather than something an admin switches on, so on a current org the diagnosis matters more than the toggle.

Every Contact insert has to lock its parent Account so the roll-up summary can recompute. In parallel mode, several batches can hold contacts for the same Account at once, and one of them loses the race. Serial mode processes "one batch must complete before the next batch starts", and a smaller batch holds each parent lock for less time — which is the Bulk API guide's own remedy when lock timeouts survive batch reorganisation (C).
Parallel mode with smaller batches (B) shrinks the window without removing the overlap. The Data Loader (A) runs on the same APIs and changes nothing about locking. And there is no defer-roll-up-summary control (D) — deferral exists for sharing calculations, not for roll-ups.
The cheaper fix to reach for first, if you control the file: sort the Contacts by AccountId so all children of one Account land in the same batch, which the guide recommends before dropping to serial mode.

The requirement that decides this is fee-based support: service contracts and entitlements are Service Cloud functionality, and the Service Cloud feature license is what turns them on for a user. Case management and knowledge for the white papers come with it.
A Lightning Platform Starter licence (A) does not include the standard CRM service objects. Sales Cloud (D) is the wrong half of the product. The plain "Salesforce" user licence (C) is the base licence Service Cloud sits on top of, so naming it alone leaves the entitlement capability unaccounted for.
Licensing is the area of Salesforce that changes most often and is packaged commercially rather than documented as a rule, so verify the current bundle against Salesforce's licence documentation before relying on this.

Two of the three are documented word for word in the LDV guide's Loading Data from the API: "Use the defer sharing calculation permission to defer sharing calculations until after all data has been loaded" (D), and "Disable Apex triggers, workflow rules, and validations during loads; investigate the use of batch Apex to process records after the load is complete" (E). Salesforce's own Extreme Data Loading series adds that sharing rules and complex relationships should be configured after the load rather than before it.
The time zone of the loading user (A) affects how date values are interpreted, not throughput. Whether the legacy system is still running (C) is a cutover question, not a performance one.
Option B is the item's weak point: removing custom indexes before a load is not among the pre-load steps Salesforce documents. Its published lean-configuration advice covers the sharing model, sharing rules, object relationships, workflow, validation, and triggers — indexes are discussed only as something to add for query speed.
findings.note: Answer stands as keyed, but option B is unsupported: the old explanation asserted that dropping custom indexes avoids per-insert index maintenance, and that step does not appear in Salesforce's documented pre-load configuration advice.

findings.explanation:
The requirement is exploration, not display: drill down, build a view on the spot, add an ad-hoc filter from a phone. CRM Analytics (Analytics Cloud) is the Salesforce product built for that interaction model, with lenses created on the fly against a dataset (D).
A standard dashboard (C) renders components from saved reports with filters an admin defined in advance; a user cannot invent a new lens from it. The external-tool options (A, B) put the data and the security model outside Salesforce and hand the user a non-native mobile experience.
Product naming here has moved more than once — Wave, Einstein Analytics, Tableau CRM, CRM Analytics — so read option D as naming the Salesforce analytics product rather than a current brand.

Classic Encryption masks an encrypted custom field's value from anyone without the "View Encrypted Data" permission, and an export runs as the exporting user, so the export inherits that masking. Granting View Encrypted Data to the user that runs the weekly export is what makes the exported values readable.
The reason to build a custom profile (D) rather than reuse a standard one (A) is that standard profiles cannot be edited — permissions on them are fixed, so there is nowhere to add the permission. Copying plaintext into a second field (B) defeats the encryption entirely and doubles the exposure. Decrypting in Apex (C) rebuilds a permission the platform already has.
Worth noting: this item is about Classic Encryption, a legacy feature. Shield Platform Encryption handles the same problem through a different permission model.

A hierarchy is expressed by pointing each record at its parent, so a self-referential custom lookup on Product2 that references the parent Product (B) reproduces the tree from the master system, and each product's children fall out as its related list.
Pointing at a child (A, C) can only ever record one child per product, which is the wrong end of a one-to-many. Master-detail is not available here for a second reason: Product2 is one of the standard objects that cannot sit on the detail side of a master-detail relationship. The Product Family picklist (D) is a flat category, not a hierarchy, and no trigger makes it into one.

Cross-system reporting needs a key that means the same thing in every system and never changes. A global unique customer number issued by the MDM hub is that key: it is the golden record's identifier, and each source system's record id maps to it, so a report can join billing, support, and CRM rows for one customer.
Email (B), phone (C), and full name (D) are all attributes a customer can change, share, or duplicate. Joining on any of them produces both missed matches and false ones, which is the problem MDM was brought in to solve.
An external ID field on the Salesforce side is where that key lives — external ID fields are indexed and support upsert, which is what keeps the mapping usable during integration.

All three keyed properties are stated on the Skinny Tables page. Salesforce "can create skinny tables to contain frequently used fields and to avoid joins" (A) — the join avoided is between an object's base table and its custom-field table. "Skinny tables are kept in sync with their source tables when the source tables are modified" (D). And they "omit soft-deleted records", so recycle-bin rows never enter a scan (E).
Option C inverts the documented rule: "Skinny tables can't contain fields from other objects." Option B invents a capability — a skinny table is a denormalised copy, not an indexing mechanism, and multi-select picklists are not something it indexes.
Two details worth carrying: the documented cap is 200 columns, and you cannot build one yourself — "You can't create, access, or modify skinny tables yourself"; Salesforce Customer Support enables them.

The stem names two distinct qualities and each keyed option measures exactly one. Completeness is the share of records where a key field is empty, which a percent-of-blanks report gives directly (C). Consistency is whether the same real value is recorded the same way, which shows up when you group a report by a key field and see how many distinct values it has actually accumulated (B).
Last-modified dates (A) measure staleness, a third quality nobody asked about. Filling blanks with defaults (D) is remediation — it changes the data instead of reviewing it, and it makes the completeness measurement look better without any of the missing information having arrived.

A data dictionary needs both halves of the picture. An entity relationship diagram (C) records how the business entities relate to one another, which is the part no schema dump gives you. The Salesforce Metadata API (D) extracts the technical definitions — objects, fields, types, help text, and the data-classification attributes on each field — so the dictionary reflects what is actually deployed rather than what someone remembers.
SOQL (A) queries records, not schema, so it cannot describe a field that holds no data yet.
Be aware this item is loose: option B, a data definition language, is a perfectly ordinary way to capture entity definitions in a data dictionary outside Salesforce, and the stem asks about "the different applications and systems used within the company", not about Salesforce alone. B is rejected here only because the item is scoped to Salesforce metadata in practice.
findings.note: Item defect: distractor B (a data definition language) is a standard data-dictionary technique for a multi-system landscape, which is what the stem describes. The key is the exam's; the item is not cleanly decidable.

findings.explanation:
Point-to-point integrations keep systems talking without ever deciding who is right, so every pair can drift independently and the customer sees a different answer depending on which system served them. An MDM solution acting as the customer master fixes the cause: one governed record, survivorship rules that decide which value wins, and centralised integrations so every system reads the same answer.
Improving the existing links (A) makes the same architecture faster at propagating disagreement. A one-time reconciliation (C) fixes today and nothing after it. Cleansing each system separately (B) leaves all of them independently authoritative, which is exactly the condition producing the complaints.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents governance practice rather than naming MDM as the answer here.

Salesforce's privacy model is built around a single standard entity rather than a preference field on each object. The Individual record is where a person's data privacy and communication preferences live, and the consent data model hangs the rest — authorization form consent, contact point consent, data use purpose — off it. Relating Leads, Person Accounts, Contacts, and Users to Individual records gives one preference store that behaves the same way for every actor type (D).
Custom fields per object (A) means four copies of the same preference and four places to keep them honest. A bespoke custom object (C) rebuilds Individual with none of the standard consent objects that already work with it. Cases (B) are a service construct and have no role in preference management.

The prospects in these CSV files are marketing audience, not sales pipeline — nobody in Sales Cloud works them until one converts. Loading them straight into Marketing Cloud (C) puts the audience where the communications are sent from and keeps the growth out of Sales Cloud storage entirely; a reconciliation process brings across only the prospects that actually become customers.
Routing the files through CRM Analytics (A) or an external database (B) still needs a second hop into Marketing Cloud and adds a system to operate. Continuing to load Leads and delete them after each sync (D) keeps every one of the storage, automation, and audit costs the stem is trying to escape, and adds a bulk delete every week.
This is a cross-cloud architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents the products rather than ranking these options.

External objects hold no data — every report row is fetched live by a web-service callout to the EDW at the moment the report runs. Thousands of reports a day across 10 to 15 external objects therefore turns directly into callout volume, and Salesforce meters it: "Depending on your qualified Salesforce organization edition, specific governor limits are in place for number of allowed callouts per hour and per day." Exceed them and the org becomes "temporarily unable to access external data sources through Salesforce Connect" — reporting stops org-wide, not just for the offending report.
The maximum records a query returns (A), the server-driven page size (C), and the ceiling on external objects per org (D) are all real limits, but none of them scales with how many times a day the reports run, which is the variable the stem puts in front of you.

A query timeout on a 50-million-row extract is a selectivity problem, and Salesforce publishes the technique that fixes it. Its LDV extraction guidance has you create an auto-number field with "Generate Auto Number for existing records" enabled, add a numeric formula field over it — because "you cannot use an index with comparison operators such as '<=' or '>' for the text-based auto-number field" — have Support index that formula field, then extract in ranges: WHERE ExportID__c > 1000000 AND ExportID__c <= 1200000. Each query stays under the index selectivity threshold, so none of them times out. That is option A, described almost word for word.
An ETL tool (C) is how you would orchestrate and schedule the extract, but on its own it issues the same unselective SOQL against the same 50 million rows and hits the same timeout — the chunking is the fix, not the tool. The REST API does not "automatically chunk records by 200" (B); that number is a query-locator page size and has nothing to do with query execution time. And the SOQL query timeout is not a value Salesforce Support raises on request (D).
On a current org, PK Chunking with the Bulk API does the same job with no custom fields, and Salesforce recommends enabling it "when querying tables with more than 10 million records or when a bulk query consistently times out". It is not among the options here, but it is what you would reach for first.
findings.note: Key moved C to A. Salesforce's own large-data-volume extraction guidance documents the auto-number plus indexed formula field as the chunking technique for exactly this failure, while an ETL tool by itself issues the same unselective query and hits the same timeout. The old explanation dismissed the documented technique as "fragile to build".

findings.explanation:
Two different causes need two different fixes. The duplicates and the disagreement about which Account is right come from having no authority: integrating Salesforce with the ERP and naming the ERP the system of truth (B) settles that. The duplicates already in Salesforce, and the ones reps will create tomorrow, need a de-duplication solution plus clear account ownership so somebody is accountable for each record (D).
A nightly de-dupe and merge job (A) cleans up after a cause nobody addressed. A one-way nightly sync (C) is half of B — it moves data without establishing that the ERP's version wins.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents duplicate management and integration mechanisms rather than ranking these pairings.

The stem already names PPS as the trusted source for Opportunity Amount, so the design question is not who wins but how to stop the argument. Removing edit access to Amount from sales users through field-level security (C) does that at the platform level, and Forecasts keep reading the same standard Amount field they always did.
Moving either party to a custom field (A, D) leaves the standard Amount — the field Opportunity Forecasting actually uses — populated by only one of the two, so either forecasts lose the trusted number or they lose the sales users' input entirely. Writing only when Amount is null (B) hands authority to whoever types first, which is the opposite of what the stem says PPS is for.

Native Duplicate Management (A) is the platform answer: matching rules decide what counts as the same customer and duplicate rules alert or block at the moment of entry, in the UI and through the API, without code.
An enterprise service bus (B) moves messages between systems and a data warehouse (D) stores copies for analysis; neither compares two customer records or prevents a third.
Option C names Data.com Clean, which Salesforce has retired — it appears in the Past Product & Feature Retirements list, and its setup article no longer exists. Keep C as the keyed answer because that is what the item tests, but the current equivalent is a third-party enrichment and cleansing service or Data Cloud, and the point that survives is the design one: preventing duplicates at entry and standardising incoming values are two different jobs, and a duplicate rule only does the first.
findings.note: Answer stands as the exam keys it, but the item is stale: keyed option C names Data.com Clean, a product Salesforce has retired.

findings.explanation:
Apex can report its own failures by email — a batch job marked Database.Stateful can accumulate failed rows across execute() calls and send them from finish() with Messaging.SingleEmailMessage, which puts the errors in front of the business team without anyone logging into Salesforce (C).
Storing the leads themselves in a custom object (A) records what did not get processed but reports no reason, and cleansing input with an AppExchange package (D) reduces failures rather than reporting them.
Be aware this item is weakly constructed. Option B — writing Apex errors to a custom object and reporting on it — is the pattern most production orgs actually use, because it survives inbox rules and supports trend reporting, and it is a direct answer to "errors should be reported to them". Nothing in the stem chooses between push and pull, so both B and C are defensible.
findings.note: Item defect: distractor B (log Apex errors to a custom object and report on it) answers the stem as well as the keyed option C does, and nothing in the question distinguishes a pushed notification from a queryable error log.

findings.explanation:
The requirement has two halves — ongoing enrichment and cleansing of 100,000 Accounts, and easy monitoring of data quality metrics — and the item wants the declarative option that covers both rather than code that covers one. Batch Apex (B) and an Account trigger (D) both mean building and maintaining an integration, plus whatever reporting you write on top of it. Prospector (C) is the wrong half of the old product pair: it adds new records rather than cleaning existing ones.
The keyed answer names Data.com Clean, and that product no longer exists — Data.com appears in Salesforce's Past Product & Feature Retirements list, and its setup article is gone. As printed, this question has no correct answer on a current org. The durable point is the shape of the right solution: a configured, scheduled enrichment service that writes back match and fill status you can report on, which today means a third-party data quality service or Data Cloud rather than anything native.
findings.note: Item is stale beyond repair: the keyed answer A is Data.com Clean, a retired product, and no remaining option is correct on a current org. Kept as keyed because that is what the exam tests.

findings.explanation:
The LDV guide's extraction advice points straight at the Bulk API: when a query could return over a million records, evaluate Bulk API 2.0's query capability. It runs asynchronously and returns results in batches, so the extract never sits inside a synchronous request waiting to time out (B).
The SOAP API (A) holds a synchronous connection open for a query it was never sized for. GZIP compression (C) makes the response smaller on the wire and changes nothing about how long the query takes to run server-side. Batch Apex (D) processes records inside Salesforce; it is not an export path to an external BI system.

One user owning every loaded Account is ownership data skew — Salesforce defines it as "a single user owns more than 10,000 records of an object" — and the cost lands on sharing recalculation: moving that user, or changing anything about their access, forces Salesforce to "adjust a very large number of entries in the sharing tables".
The documented mitigation is exact. First choice: "If you do have a compelling reason for assigning ownership to a small number of users, you can minimize possible performance impacts by not assigning the users to a role" — that is option A. If the user must have a role, the guidance is "Place them in a separate role at the top of the hierarchy", then "Don't move them out of that top-level role to avoid triggering sharing recalculations" — that is option D.
Option B does the opposite of what is documented. A role at the bottom of the hierarchy means every role above it inherits access to all of those records, so the sharing tables carry an entry for each ancestor and every recalculation walks the whole hierarchy. Option C is worse still: a real VP reporting to a senior VP sits mid-hierarchy and is a person whose role will actually change.
The same page adds a third rule worth remembering: "Keep them out of public groups that can be used as the source for sharing rules."
findings.note: Key moved A,B to A,D. Salesforce's Ownership Data Skew page says to place a heavy-owning user in "a separate role at the top of the hierarchy" when a role is unavoidable. The deck keyed the lowest-level role, which is the placement that maximises sharing-table entries because every role above inherits access to all the records.

findings.explanation:
A report in an external BI tool (A) reads Account data from Salesforce and Invoice data from the ERP directly, with no dependency on the external-object layer at all. A Visualforce page (C) queries the Account and the Invoice external object together and renders them as one view inside Salesforce.
Two separate reports side by side on a dashboard (D) is explicitly not the single combined report the stem asks for.
Option B is the interesting one. Salesforce does support reporting on external objects — it publishes an article titled "Salesforce Connect Support for Reports" — so a custom report type spanning Account and an Invoices external object is possible in principle. It needs an external lookup or indirect lookup relationship between them, which this stem never says exists, and reports that touch an external object are bounded in how many rows they fetch and depend on the ERP responding while the report runs. That is why A and C are the safer recommendations here, not because native reporting on external objects is impossible.
findings.note: Answer stands, but the old explanation asserted that "Salesforce cannot natively report across a standard object and an external object together" — an invented absence. Salesforce publishes "Salesforce Connect Support for Reports"; option B is possible given a lookup relationship, so this item has three defensible options rather than two.

findings.explanation:
Traceability needs the reason to travel with the thing that changed. A field's Description holds its business purpose on the metadata itself, so it survives every deployment and is visible to whoever finds the field later (B). Metadata files in source control record exactly what changed in each of the three releases, and the commit history carries the why alongside it (D).
The setup audit trail (A) is a genuine record of what changed and when, but it captures no link to a requirement — it will tell you a field was created and by whom, never which documented requirement asked for it.
Be aware this item is loose: option C, a data dictionary holding the justification for each field, is a direct answer to "trace back configuration changes to the detailed requirements" and is a technique Salesforce's own governance guidance recommends. Nothing in the stem separates it from B, so three of the four options are defensible.
findings.note: Item defect: distractor C (maintain a data dictionary with the justification for each field) answers the stem as directly as keyed option B, and Salesforce's governance guidance recommends exactly that. The key is the exam's; the item is not cleanly decidable.

findings.explanation:
One hundred million cases a month is far outside what the transactional store is designed to report on, and big objects are the platform's answer to that shape — "consistent performance, whether you have 1 million records, 100 million, or even 1 billion", with "Historical archive" and "360° view of the customer" as their named use cases. Archive the case volume there and run the analysis on the analytics platform (B).
Out-of-the-box reports over standard Cases (D) are the thing that has already stopped working at this volume. Rolling everything into aggregate custom objects (C) means building and maintaining the aggregation yourself, and loses the detail behind it. Moving to a warehouse (A) works but takes the data off-platform, which the stem does not ask for.
One implementation detail: Salesforce does not have you report directly off a big object. View Big Object Data in Reports and Dashboards has you extract a representative subset — with Bulk API or batch Apex — into a custom object or dataset, and analyse that.

Persistent group-membership lock errors come from the sharing system locking "the tables holding group membership information during updates to prevent incompatible simultaneous updates". Granular locking is the mechanism that narrows those locks so "some group maintenance operations to proceed simultaneously if there's no hierarchical or other relationship between the roles or groups involved" — which is exactly what lets a manual update and an automated one run at the same time (A).
Deferring sharing calculation (C) is a planned bulk-window tool: you suspend recalculation, do the work, resume. It does not make two concurrent membership updates compatible. Parallel sharing rule recalculation (B) speeds recalculation of sharing rules, a different operation from group membership. Implicit sharing (D) is how Salesforce grants parent access from child records; it has no bearing on locking.
One currency note: Salesforce now documents granular locking as the default behaviour rather than something an admin turns on.

Franchisees tracking customer sales and opportunities are partners, not customers, and that distinction is what the licence split is built on: the Partner Community licence is the external licence that carries leads, opportunities, campaigns, and quotes, along with reports and dashboards in the site. Customer Community (C) is built for service — cases, knowledge, orders — and does not extend to the sales objects these franchisees need.
A full Salesforce licence (A) is for internal employees and would not be bought a thousand times over for external franchisees. A Lightning Platform licence (B) gives custom apps without the standard CRM sales objects.
Licensing is packaged commercially and changes often, so confirm the current Experience Cloud licence comparison before relying on this.

Once native reports and dashboards have hit their ceiling, the two directions that add real analytical capability are the Salesforce analytics platform — CRM Analytics, named here by its older brand — which brings datasets, lenses, and exploration beyond what a report can express (B), and purpose-built analytics apps from AppExchange that package models and dashboards for a domain (A).
Weekly snapshots (C) are a way to accumulate history for trending; useful, but they add data, not analytical capability. The Setup Audit Trail (D) records configuration changes and has nothing to do with business insight.
The product in option B has been renamed several times — Wave, Einstein Analytics, Tableau CRM, CRM Analytics — so read it as naming the Salesforce analytics platform rather than a current brand.

Big objects sit outside the standard reporting path. Salesforce's own guidance is that at this scale "it's not practical to build reports or dashboards directly from that data" — you extract a representative subset into a custom object and report on that (B), or feed the analytics platform and analyse it there (D). Standard reports and dashboards (A) cannot be pointed at a big object, and synchronous SOQL (C) is confined to the big object's index fields with equality and range filters only, which is a lookup mechanism rather than a reporting one.
Read option B for the pattern, not the tool it names. **Async SOQL was retired in Summer '23**: Salesforce's retirement notice states "You must use the Bulk API or batch Apex to query or report on custom Big Objects after your org gets upgraded to the Summer '23 release." The aggregate-into-a-custom-object approach is still right; the mechanism is now Bulk API or batch Apex.
findings.note: Answer stands as keyed, but keyed option B names Async SOQL, which Salesforce retired in Summer '23 and replaced with Bulk API or batch Apex for querying and reporting on big objects.

findings.explanation:
Overwriting temperature and humidity on the Container record (A) keeps only the latest value, and the stem requires historical readings as well as current ones — so the readings have to be their own records. A Container Reading child object gives that, and the archiving process is what keeps it viable: 50,000 containers reporting every ten minutes is 144 readings per container per day, so each Container passes 10,000 children in under three months. Salesforce's own guidance is to "Distribute child records so that no parent has more than 10,000 child records", which makes an archiving process part of the design rather than an optimisation (D).
Option B is the same model without that archiving, so it walks into parent-child data skew on every container. A Lightning component reading from the warehouse (C) solves the display problem and never stores the current reading in Salesforce at all.

A governance programme exists to make data trustworthy and useful. Integrity (A) is the trustworthy half — accuracy, consistency, and validity of the values themselves. Usability (C) is the other half — data that people can find, interpret the same way, and reuse, which is why governance produces things like a data dictionary and field-level classification rather than only validation rules.
Distribution (B) and modelling (D) are how the data gets built and moved. Both are shaped by governance decisions; neither is an outcome the programme is measured on.
This is a definitional item drawn from general data-governance practice rather than a Salesforce rule.

MDM enforces a decision about which system owns a field; it does not make that decision. Two systems whose fields share a purpose have to be compared by the people who know how each is populated and what the field will be used for in Salesforce, and that review is what produces a field-level system of record (B).
Option A hands the judgment to the tool, which is precisely the step MDM cannot do for you. Option C makes a naming difference into a schema difference, which manufactures duplicate fields for the same concept. Option D describes last-writer-wins and then declares the problem unsolvable — the ungoverned outcome the whole exercise exists to prevent.
This is a governance-judgment item; Salesforce documents the mechanisms rather than the review.

Standard field history tracking cannot reach 100 fields — "The default limit is 20 fields per object" — and what it does capture is retained for a bounded window rather than indefinitely. So option D is not a configuration anyone can save, and the requirement has to be met by writing the history yourself.
Both remaining approaches do that. A custom object that stores a copy of the record whenever it changes (A) preserves the whole state at each point in time. A custom object that logs the previous and new values for each changed field (B) stores the deltas, which is closer to what field history actually is and far cheaper per change. Either is populated from an Apex trigger.
Reporting snapshots (C) run on a schedule and capture report rows, so they sample state at fixed intervals — they would miss every change that happens and reverses between two runs.

A person account "stores information about individual consumers" — one record that carries both account and contact attributes, which is what a B2C model needs when there is no employing organisation to hang a Contact from (D).
Contacts alone (C), or an account-and-contact pair (B), both require a parent Account, and inventing one shared parent for consumers produces the parent-child data skew Salesforce warns against. "Individual Accounts" (A) is not a Salesforce feature; the standard object named Individual exists, but it holds data privacy and consent preferences, not the consumer's account record.
Before enabling this in a real org, read Considerations for Using Person Accounts — the feature changes Account behaviour org-wide and cannot be turned off.

The LDV guide's reporting advice is to cut both joins and rows. Denormalising the related data onto the Account with triggers (A) is its "De-normalize data when practical… Use summarized data stored on the parent record for the report" — the report then reads one object instead of joining Contact, Opportunity, and Order across several million Accounts. An indexed date field with a bounded filter (D) is the other half: "Use report filters that emphasize the use of standard or custom indexed fields", and a bounded range is what lets the optimizer use that index.
Cross-object formula fields (B) are evaluated at query time on every row, so they add the join cost back that denormalising removed. Unbounded date ranges (C) defeat index selectivity outright and send the query to a full scan.

The adoption problem here is that the reps' actual working data never arrived. Defining a standard field mapping from the spreadsheets to Opportunity and training the teams to import their own data (B) puts that history into Salesforce and, just as importantly, leaves the reps able to do it again without filing a ticket.
An Excel connector syncing individual files (A) keeps the spreadsheets authoritative, which is the habit the implementation was meant to end. An external database (C) adds a system nobody asked for. Uploading the files to a Chatter group (D) stores them as attachments — not reportable, not forecastable, and no better than the shared drive they came from.
This is a change-adoption judgment item rather than a documented rule.

Monitoring means something that keeps producing numbers without anyone remembering to run it. Reports and dashboards built on the quality dimensions the org cares about (B) do that natively, and the Data Quality Analysis Dashboards app from Salesforce Labs (C) packages the same idea — formula fields that score completeness on Leads, Accounts, Contacts, Opportunities and more, surfaced as dashboards — free, and installable without building it yourself.
Custom objects and fields to "identify issues" (A) is a build with no measurement attached. Exporting and checking outside Salesforce (D) is a one-off audit that tells the sales managers nothing next month.

Salesforce's default advice runs the other way — "Unless the data absolutely needs to reside in Salesforce, consider data virtualization with Salesforce Connect instead", because "More data in your organization ultimately leads to larger data volumes, which can adversely affect performance and add technical debt." What makes this stem an exception is its third requirement.
Reporting alone might survive virtualization. Programmatic aggregation and workflow participation do not: external objects do not support Apex triggers, and the automation surface over them is narrow. Once developers need to aggregate the records in Apex and feed them into workflows, the data has to be persisted in Salesforce objects (D).
Bidirectional and unidirectional (A, B) describe which way data flows, not whether it is stored — they answer a different question than the one asked.

Field-level audit and recovery means keeping the old values, not just the current ones, and keeping them long enough to recover from something noticed weeks later. That is a storage question before it is a tooling one, so projecting the storage the retained history and backup copies will consume is the design consideration the plan turns on (C).
Purging old data (A) is the opposite of what a recovery plan needs. A weekly export (D) has a seven-day blast radius and no field-level granularity — it restores a record as it was last Saturday, not the one field somebody corrupted on Wednesday.
Be aware the item is loose. Option B, an AppExchange backup package, is how most orgs actually get granular field-level recovery, and it answers "what should the architect consider" nearly as directly as C does. C is keyed because it names a planning input rather than a product, but the two are not cleanly separated by the stem.
findings.note: Item defect: distractor B (an AppExchange backup package) is a reasonable answer to "what should the architect consider" for granular field-level recovery, and nothing in the stem separates a planning input from a tooling choice.

findings.explanation:
Two of the four requirements pick the relationship between them. Access parity — VTOTime__c must be viewable and editable exactly as its Project__c is — comes free with master-detail, because detail records "inherit the master's sharing and security settings". Total hours on the Project record needs a roll-up summary, and roll-up summary fields require a master-detail relationship. Both point at C.
The direction matters and options D and A get it backwards: the master-detail field lives on the detail object, so it belongs on VTOTime__c pointing at Project__c, not the reverse. And a formula field on Project__c (B) evaluates against its own record — it cannot sum values across child records, which is precisely the job roll-up summary exists for.

Salesforce requires approval before you load-test the platform, and the requirement is concrete: "Submit an LAP request for approval at least one week before the testing date", with a test plan document, dates, sandbox org id, business scenario and justification. "All tests must be pre-approved. Unapproved testing is subject to throttling or blocking." That settles B. And the applications worth putting through this are the ones whose behaviour is not already known — heavy custom code, or large data volumes (C).
Option A is not merely an overstatement; it describes something Salesforce forbids. "Because Salesforce is a multitenant platform, performance testing is not permitted in production environments. Use a full copy sandbox for testing", and "scale tests are only permitted in sandboxes." Option D fails for the reason a full copy sandbox is specified in the first place: a sandbox with different data volumes is not a predictor of production.
findings.note: Answer stands. The old explanation rejected option A with "not all apps must be tested in both environments", which leaves a learner believing production performance testing is sometimes required. Salesforce does not permit performance testing in production at all — it is sandbox-only, and every test needs prior approval.

findings.explanation:
Two systems are live and both can write, so the first thing to settle is who is right today: naming the legacy CRM the system of record for the transition period (B) removes the ambiguity while the remaining users are still on it. The second is who will be right tomorrow, per object and per field, as functionality moves across — that is what an MDM plan agreed with stakeholders gives you (C), and it is the part that survives the legacy system's retirement.
Replicating legacy changes into Salesforce (A) is a mechanism you might well implement, but it presumes the authority question is already answered. Refusing to connect the two CRMs (D) is a routing rule, not a governance decision, and it leaves the ERP mediating conflicts nobody has adjudicated.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents the integration mechanisms rather than ranking these choices.

"All systems have access to the same customer information" is a consistency requirement, and consistency needs an arbiter. An MDM strategy supplies one: a golden customer record with survivorship rules deciding which system's value wins for each attribute, which every system then reads (B).
Declaring Salesforce the system of record for everything (A) is a decision made before looking at which system is actually authoritative for which data. Loading the customer data into every system (C) creates the copies that drift. Letting each system own what it generates (D) is a reasonable-sounding rule that reproduces exactly the silos the stem is complaining about — the customer's address exists in three places and no rule says which one is current.
This is an architecture-judgment item; Salesforce documents integration mechanisms rather than naming MDM as the answer here.

Defining quality standards means naming the dimensions you will hold the data to and how each is measured. Duplication standards and matching rules (A) define what counts as the same record. Timeliness and consistency (C) cover how current a value must be and whether the same fact is recorded the same way everywhere. Completeness and accuracy (E) cover whether required information is present and correct — the two complaints the stem actually names.
Picking key fields in a staging database (B) and choosing an ETL tool (D) are migration decisions. They matter, but they belong to how data moves, not to what "good" means, and neither would appear in a standards document.
This is a definitional item drawn from general data-governance practice rather than a Salesforce rule.

Leads, opportunities, and orders are sales objects, and the Partner Community licence is the external licence that carries them along with reports and dashboards in the site (D). That combination is what a channel sales portal for resellers needs, and it is the line that separates this licence from the customer-facing ones.
Customer Community and Customer Community Plus (A, C) are built for service — cases, knowledge, orders — and do not extend to leads and opportunities. Lightning External Apps Starter (B) is sized for custom apps rather than CRM sales objects with reporting.
The stem's fourth requirement — no more than 10 custom objects and no extra file storage — is there to tell you the cheaper external licences are not being ruled out by object count, so the sales objects and reporting are what decide it.
Licensing is packaged commercially and changes often, so confirm the current Experience Cloud licence comparison before relying on this.

Required on a page layout is a UI rule. It applies to the users looking at that layout and to nothing else, so an integration writing through the API sails past it — which is exactly what is happening here.
Both keyed options work at a level the API cannot bypass. Marking the field required at the field level makes it universally required, and a universally required field "must have a value whenever a record is saved within Salesforce, the Lightning Platform API, Connect Offline, Salesforce for Outlook, the Self-Service portal, or automated processes" (C). A validation rule rejecting blank values (A) runs on every save path too, and gives a message naming the problem.
Defaulting a value when the field is blank (B) makes the records look complete while losing the fact that the source system sent nothing — the opposite of ensuring the data comes from the source. Option D is not an approach.
